description: Interethnic friendship among children In contemporary classrooms children are increasingly exposed to ethnic diversity, which presents both challenges and opportunities for social development. The 38 studies in this cluster, represented by red color in Fig. 4, investigate interethnic friendships among children, focusing on their dynamics, benefits, and influencing factors. These studies reveal that although cross-ethnic friendships may show less stability compared to same-ethnic ones, they are instrumental in fostering several positive outcomes. Key benefits identified include enhanced intergroup attitudes (Chen & Graham, 2015), reduction in perceived vulnerability (Graham et al., 2013), and notable improvements in academic engagement, peer acceptance, and emotional well-being (Kawabata & Crick, 2015). Further, such friendships contribute to the development of complex social identities and fortify the sense of community among peers (Serdiouk et al., 2022). The research also shed light on various predictors that facilitate the formation of cross-ethnic friendships. These include children’s self-efficacy beliefs in forming and maintaining these friendships (Bagci et al., 2022), their ability to take the perspective of others (Chávez et al., 2021), and the value they place on diversity (Bahns, 2017). Parental attitudes and behaviors, interactions beyond the school environment, school norms, and positive intergroup contact attitudes also play crucial roles (Lessard et al., 2018; RivasDrake et al., 2018). Notably, the studies emphasize the significance of the socialization context in shaping interethnic friendships. This context includes interactions with peers, parental influences, and teacher-student dynamics (Miklikowska, 2017). Additionally, the research advocates for inclusive educational practices that not only encourage cross-ethnic friendships but also promote broader social harmony (Juvonen et al., 2019).

Cross-Group Friendships as Catalyst for Integration and Change Represented by green color in Fig. 4, this cluster of 36 studies delves into the transformative potential of cross-group friendships on societal integration and change. The research encompasses diverse populations, including LGBTQ individuals (Bagci et al., 2020), physically disabled people (Bagci et al., 2018), residents of highly prejudiced societies, refugees, and other minority groups (Bagci et al., 2019). These studies highlight the multifaceted benefits of crossgroup friendships. Key findings include the association of cross-group friendships with higher cognitive flexibility (Bagci et al., 2019), support for multiculturalism (Bagci & Çelebi, 2017), and reduced homophobic attitudes (Bagci et al., 2020). Cross-group friendships also foster motivation to cooperate and enhance social integration (Fasbender & Drury, 2021). However, the positive impacts of these friendships can be mitigated by factors such as perceived interethnic conflict (Bagci & Çelebi, 2016) and entrenched group-based ideologies like ethnocentrism and social dominance orientation (Bagci et al., 2019). Furthermore, these studies explore the influence of crossgroup friendships on broader societal actions. For instance, they have been linked to increased willingness for collective action (Becker et al., 2013), greater intergroup forgiveness (Voci et al., 2015), and support for inclusive policies (MacInnis & Hodson, 2018). Notably, cross-group friendships that recognize and challenge group inequalities foster positive intergroup attitudes and proactive behaviours. However, such friendships can inadvertently undermine collective action among disadvantaged groups if members of advantaged groups perceive their status as legitimate or remain ambiguous about intergroup inequalities (Becker et al., 2013). Additionally, some studies in this cluster focus on intervention programs designed to bridge social divides. One such intervention tested imagined contact scenarios with friendship potential among Turkish residents and Syrian refugees, showing positive outcomes in attitudes, trust, behavioural intentions, and perceived threat reduction (Bagci et al., 2017). Another significant intervention was a coexistence program for Israeli and Palestinian teenagers, which demonstrated that outgroup friendships formed during the program led to increased positivity toward outgroup members and generalized positive feelings (Schroeder & Risen, 2014).

Recent advances in intergroup contact theory Represented by blue in Fig. 4, this cluster of 26 studies delves into the evolving dynamics of intergroup contact theory, reflecting the current global context of increased migration and diversification of social interactions. These studies extend beyond traditional direct friendships, exploring a range of indirect cross-group contacts and their influence on intergroup relations. Key forms of indirect contact include extended (Zhou et al., 2018), imagined (Vezzali et al., 2019), and virtual contacts (Schwab & Greitemeyer, 2014), each demonstrating significant impact on altering outgroup attitudes (Zhou et al., 2018), promoting outgroup humanization (Capozza et al., 2020), and enhancing social inclusion (Grütter et al., 2017). The research encompasses an array of populations, including homosexuals (Vezzali et al., 2016a, b), children with special educational needs (Grütter & Meyer, 2014), and diverse ethnic groups, such as immigrants (Vezzali & Stathi, 2016). Pioneering interventions aimed at fostering social inclusion have been tested, ranging from behavioural journalism (Liebkind et al., 2013) and imagined intergroup contact (Vezzali et al., 2019), to educational initiatives like essay-based interventions in schools (Vezzali et al., 2015). These innovative approaches have yielded promising outcomes, such as heightened willingness to engage in cross-group friendships (Vezzali et al., 2015), reduction in tendencies toward social exclusion and bullying (Vezzali et al., 2019), and heightened recognition of the importance of intergroup contact for future societal cohesion (Liebkind et al., 2013). Moreover, this body of research sheds light on the intricate interplay of situational and personal factors in shaping cross-group friendships. Situational influences encompass a variety of elements, including the presence of supportive social norms (Gómez et al., 2018), educators’ attitudes towards diversity (Grütter & Meyer, 2014), and the influence of parental cross-group friendships (Meeusen, 2014). Concurrently, personal attributes such as social dominance orientation (Trifiletti et al., 2019) and an individual’s confidence in engaging in contact (Turner & Cameron, 2016) have emerged as crucial predictors of the formation and success of these friendships.
